thesis_at_purchase_vs_now: Original thesis: commodity producer bought at a significant price-to-value gap [D07].
Current status: market value and oil price have caught up to our estimate of intrinsic value [D02], [D05].
final.price_vs_value_now: The stock trades at approximately 14.53x earnings and 3.50x book value [D04], reflecting a valuation where the original discount has been largely eliminated by rising profits and market appreciation [D02].
final.after_tax_hurdle: Realizing the substantial gain requires paying a 35% federal tax rate [D08], but the current valuation now fully reflects the business's earning power, making further holding unattractive relative to other capital uses [D04], [D06].

drivers.driver: The original price-to-value gap that motivated the purchase has closed as market valuations caught up with our appraisal [D02], [D07].
The business's profitability is highly sensitive to commodity cycles, and current earnings are capitalized at levels that do not provide a sufficient margin of safety [D04], [D05].
Alternative uses for capital, including Berkshire's other high-quality holdings or cash, now offer more attractive risk-adjusted prospects given the full valuation of this position [D06], [D08].

final.memo:
We purchased our stake in PetroChina during 2002–2003 because the market significantly undervalued the company's assets and earning power [D07]. At that time, we were buying a producer of a vital commodity at a price that offered a clear and substantial margin of safety [D07]. Today, the situation has changed. Our evaluation of the business and the current oil price suggests that the market value has caught up with our estimate of intrinsic value [D05]. 

While the company has demonstrated record profitability in recent years, we must recognize that petroleum accounting profits are heavily influenced by realized prices and volumes that do not constitute a perpetual annuity [D02], [D03]. We do not attempt to forecast the commodity, but we must acknowledge that capitalizing these earnings at current levels assumes a favorable environment that may not persist [D05]. 

We have always held that we do not sell wonderful businesses simply because Mr. Market is enthusiastic; however, this investment was made as a price-to-value gap play rather than as a permanent franchise [D04], [D07]. With the discount largely eliminated, we believe it is the right time to exit and redeploy our capital elsewhere. We recognize that selling triggers a material tax cost at the 35% rate, but we prefer to move on when the original thesis has been fulfilled rather than anchoring on historical cost [D08].
